What are the 6 Advantages of Cloud Computing?
column2:
1. Trade fixed expense (CapEx) for variable expense (OpEx)
2. Massive economies of scale
3. Stop guessing capacity
4. Increase speed and agility
5. Stop spending money running/maintaining data centers
6. Go global in minutes

column1: Define CapEx vs. OpEx in AWS Cloud Economics.
column2:
CapEx (Fixed expense): Upfront investment in physical servers/data centers.
OpEx (Variable expense): Pay-as-you-go operational spending based on actual cloud consumption.

column1: What does AWS Economies of Scale mean for customers?
column2: Because AWS aggregates usage from hundreds of thousands of customers globally, AWS achieves lower hardware/operating costs and passes those savings on as lower pay-as-you-go prices.

column1: Contrast Agility, Elasticity, and Scalability in AWS.
column2:
Agility: Provision IT resources in minutes to experiment and innovate quickly.
Elasticity: Automatically scale resources out AND in to match changing demand.
Scalability: Ability to handle growing workloads (vertically = bigger server; horizontally = more servers).

column1: Contrast High Availability (HA) vs. Fault Tolerance.
column2:
High Availability: Minimizing downtime so an app stays accessible (e.g., Multi-AZ failover with brief disruption).
Fault Tolerance: Built-in redundancy so the system keeps operating with zero/near-zero disruption even when components fail.

column1: What is the difference between Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) and Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)?
column2:
Horizontal (Scale Out/In): Add or remove instances (e.g., EC2 Auto Scaling) — cloud-native best practice.
Vertical (Scale Up/Down): Increase/decrease CPU/RAM of a single instance (hardware limit & requires restart).

column1: Name all 6 Pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
column2:
1. Operational Excellence
2. Security
3. Reliability
4. Performance Efficiency
5. Cost Optimization
6. Sustainability
Mnemonic: Our Systems Run Perfectly, Cost Smart

column1: Well-Architected Pillar: Operational Excellence — core goal and key design principles?
column2:
Goal: Run and monitor systems to deliver business value and continuously improve processes.
Principles: Perform operations as code, make frequent small reversible changes, refine procedures frequently, anticipate failure, learn from operational failures.

column1: Well-Architected Pillar: Security — core goal and key design principles?
column2:
Goal: Protect data, systems, and assets through risk assessments and mitigation.
Principles: Strong identity foundation, least privilege, enable traceability, apply security at all layers, automate security best practices, protect data in transit & at rest, keep people away from data.

column1: Well-Architected Pillar: Reliability — core goal and key design principles?
column2:
Goal: Ensure a workload performs its intended function and recovers quickly from failure.
Principles: Automatically recover from failure, test recovery procedures, scale horizontally, stop guessing capacity, manage change through automation.

column1: Well-Architected Pillar: Performance Efficiency — core goal and key design principles?
column2:
Goal: Use computing resources efficiently as demand and technology evolve.
Principles: Democratize advanced technologies (managed services), go global in minutes, use serverless architectures, experiment more often, mechanical sympathy (right tool for the job).

column1: Well-Architected Pillar: Cost Optimization — core goal and key design principles?
column2:
Goal: Run systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point.
Principles: Implement Cloud Financial Management (CFM), adopt a consumption model, measure overall efficiency, stop spending on undifferentiated heavy lifting, analyze and attribute expenditure.

column1: Well-Architected Pillar: Sustainability — core goal and key design principles?
column2:
Goal: Minimize the environmental impacts of running cloud workloads.
Principles: Understand impact, establish sustainability goals, maximize utilization (rightsizing), adopt efficient hardware/managed services, reduce downstream impact of workloads.

column1: What is the AWS Well-Architected Tool?
column2: A free AWS console service that lets you review your architectures against the 6 Well-Architected pillars, answer guided questions, and receive a prioritized improvement plan.

column1: Name the 6 Perspectives of the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) and their two groups.
column2:
Business Capabilities: Business, People, Governance
Technical Capabilities: Platform, Security, Operations
Mnemonic: Big Projects Go Pretty Smoothly Overall

column1: AWS CAF: Which perspective focuses on culture, organizational change, workforce training, and cloud fluency?
column2: People Perspective (Business Capabilities).

column1: AWS CAF: Which perspective focuses on cloud financial management, risk management, data governance, and benefits management?
column2: Governance Perspective (Business Capabilities).

column1: AWS CAF: Which perspective ensures cloud investments align with IT strategy, product management, and measurable business outcomes?
column2: Business Perspective (Business Capabilities).

column1: AWS CAF: Which perspective designs scalable enterprise-grade hybrid cloud, data, application architecture, and CI/CD pipelines?
column2: Platform Perspective (Technical Capabilities).

column1: AWS CAF: Which perspective focuses on day-to-day observability, AIOps, incident/change management, and business continuity / disaster recovery?
column2: Operations Perspective (Technical Capabilities).

column1: What are the 4 Business Value Outcomes of AWS CAF highlighted in CLF-C02 Domain 1?
column2:
1. Reduced business risk
2. Improved ESG (environmental, social, governance) performance
3. Increased revenue
4. Increased operational efficiency

column1: What are the 4 Transformation Domains of AWS CAF?
column2: Technology, Process, Organization, and Product.

column1: List the 7 Rs of AWS Cloud Migration.
column2:
1. Rehost (lift & shift)
2. Relocate (hypervisor-level lift & shift, e.g., VMware)
3. Replatform (lift, tinker & shift)
4. Repurchase (drop & shop / move to SaaS)
5. Refactor (re-architect cloud-native)
6. Retire (decommission)
7. Retain (keep on-prem for now)

column1: Migration Strategy: Moving a self-managed on-premises MySQL database onto Amazon RDS without changing app code is which of the 7 Rs?
column2: Replatform (lift, tinker, and shift) — gains managed cloud optimizations without redesigning core application architecture.

column1: Migration Strategy: Replacing a legacy self-hosted CRM with a SaaS subscription product is which of the 7 Rs?
column2: Repurchase (drop and shop).

column1: Migration Strategy: Rewriting a monolithic application into serverless AWS Lambda + Amazon DynamoDB microservices is which of the 7 Rs?
column2: Refactor / Re-architect — highest upfront effort, highest long-term cloud agility and cost efficiency.

column1: What does Rightsizing mean in AWS Cloud Economics?
column2: Matching EC2 instance types, sizes, and storage capacity to actual workload performance requirements (e.g., downsizing over-provisioned instances) to eliminate waste and cut costs.

column1: Compare BYOL (Bring Your Own License) vs. License-Included models on AWS.
column2:
BYOL: Reuse existing eligible enterprise software licenses (e.g., Windows/Oracle) on AWS (often requiring EC2 Dedicated Hosts for per-socket/core compliance).
License-Included: AWS bundles the software license into pay-as-you-go hourly pricing with no upfront licensing commitment.
